title: Calculation and application of the selenium toxicity coefficient for potential ecological risk assessment.
abstract: To address the lack of a unified quantitative index for the ecological risk assessment of selenium (Se) in soils, the toxicity coefficient of Se was first determined based on Håkanson's principles, and the spatial distribution and potential ecological risk of Se in surface soils across China were systematically evaluated. The results showed that the toxicity coefficient of Se was determined as 2. Based on the corrected background reference value, approximately 69.9% of the sampling sites were classified as low to moderate ecological risk, 24.4% as considerable risk, and 5.7% as high or very high risk. The elevated risk sites were predominantly confined to localized areas underlain by Se-rich strata, such as Enshi in Hubei Province and Ziyang in Shaanxi Province. A substantial consistency was observed between the potential ecological risk factor (Eri) and the geoaccumulation index (Igeo), with a quadratic weighted Kappa coefficient (κw) of 0.729, indicating that the two classification systems yield comparable results in terms of risk ranking. This study provides a preliminary screening benchmark for identifying areas that warrant further site-specific investigation.

title: Behavioral responses of skipjack tuna to diluted waters from the Yangtze River in the East China Sea.
abstract: This study investigated changes in the swimming behavior of skipjack tuna (Katsuwonus pelamis) in the low-salinity waters of the East China Sea (ECS), influenced by nutrient-rich freshwater from the Yangtze River, to elucidate their response to riverine freshwater. Behavioral data from 18 individuals collected through archival tag release surveys conducted around Japan's Nansei Islands were analyzed. Five individuals that experienced sea surface salinity (SSS) below 33.5 psu were identified as low-salinity-exposed individuals, and their relationships with marine environmental parameters (e.g., temperature, salinity, chlorophyll, sea surface height, and dissolved oxygen [DO]) were examined at the individual level. Furthermore, energy intake was estimated from body temperature changes, enabling comparison of swimming behavior between low-salinity environments and the open ocean from both physical and physiological perspectives. The five low-salinity-exposed individuals showed different distribution and behavioral patterns between spring (three individuals: Sp1, Sp2, and Sp3) and summer (two individuals: Su1 and Su2). In spring, skipjack tuna were observed in waters with temperatures no less than 18°C. In summer, individuals were observed in environments with DO levels mainly higher than 3.6 mL L-1 and SSS of no less than 31.3 psu. Additionally, two individuals (Sp1 and Su2) showed higher estimated energy intake in low-salinity waters compared with the open ocean (Sp1: 139.9 ± 46.0 vs. 92.3 ± 43.8 kcal/day; Su2: 210.5 ± 52.2 vs. 176.6 ± 59.3 kcal/day), while the remaining three individuals showed no significant difference or could not be compared due to very short residence time in low salinity condition. Although these results were obtained from only five individuals, the findings suggest that diluted water in the ECS may affect feeding opportunities and distribution of skipjack tuna through variability in temperature, salinity and DO.

title: WISH-barcoding of Salmonella Typhimurium ATCC14028s strains for population dynamics studies in vivo.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Barcoding of isogenic strains is a powerful approach to assess pathogen population dynamics during infection. Here, we adapted WISH-barcoding to Salmonella Typhimurium ATCC14028s to evaluate its suitability for pooled infection experiments in streptomycin-pretreated mouse models.
RESULTS: WISH-barcoded wild-type pools showed pronounced population instability, characterized by reproducible strain loss and segregation into high- and low-fitness subpopulations. Whole-genome sequencing identified recurrent mutations in the methyltransferase gene rsmG and loss of the P3 plasmid carrying streptomycin resistance in low-fitness strains; neither was observed in ΔinvG or ΔssaV pools. We propose that rsmG mutations were enriched during strain construction carried out under streptomycin selection, following loss of the P3 plasmid. Control experiments demonstrated that rsmG mutations and P3 loss are counter-selected in vivo and attenuate gut-luminal colonization in streptomycin-pretreated mice.
CONCLUSION: While population dynamics experiments with ATCC14028s are feasible in principle, wild-type strains are prone to acquiring fitness-altering mutations during in vitro construction when using the P3 plasmid and streptomycin, highlighting the need for careful pool validation prior to use and for minimizing antibiotic exposure during strain construction when the strain of interest has no natural resistance, to reduce the risk of selecting mutations.

title: Smartphone behavior and loneliness among older couples in China: Actor-partner interdependence modeling.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Much evidence suggests that smartphone behavior is associated with loneliness, but no studies have examined the relationship at the dyadic level in Chinese older couples. The aim of this study is to determine whether smartphone behavior is associated with loneliness in individuals and their spouse.
METHODS: This cross-sectional study included 202 older couples from two community healthcare centers in Chengdu, China, between October 2022 and May 2023. The actor-partner interdependence model (APIM) was constructed to investigate the interdependent effect between smartphone behavior (i.e., smartphone proficiency, smartphone duration, smartphone usage, and overall smartphone behavior score) and loneliness.
RESULTS: In terms of actor effects, husbands' smartphone proficiency, duration, usage, and overall behavior score were negatively associated with their own loneliness. For wives, however, only their smartphone proficiency, duration, and overall score showed such negative associations; no significant actor effect was found for wives' smartphone usage on their own loneliness. Regarding partner effects, some significant findings emerged: husbands' longer smartphone duration and higher overall behavior score were significantly associated with lower loneliness in their wives.
CONCLUSIONS: This research indicated the dyadic interdependence of smartphone behavior and loneliness in older couples. Future mental health interventions for the older people should treat the couple as a unit.

title: How peer behavior shapes academic misconduct: The roles of moral disengagement and shame.
abstract: Academic misconduct predisposition remains an important concern in higher education, and peer behavior perception has emerged as a relevant correlate of students' academic integrity-related tendencies. Drawing on social cognitive theory and Bandura's moral disengagement theory, this study examined how perceived peer misconduct is associated with students'self-reported predisposition toward academic misconduct through moral disengagement and shame. Data were collected through a cross-sectional survey of 418 undergraduate students from a comprehensive university in Shandong, China. Structural equation modeling and Bootstrap analyses with 5,000 resamples were used to estimate a serial mediation model. The results showed that peer behavior perception was positively associated with moral disengagement (β = .423, p < .001), moral disengagement was negatively associated with shame (β = -.223, p < .001), and shame was negatively associated with academic misconduct predisposition (β = -.309, p < .001). The direct association between peer behavior perception and academic misconduct predisposition remained statistically significant (β = .272, p < .001). Bootstrap results further showed significant indirect effects through moral disengagement, through shame, and through the serial pathway from moral disengagement to shame. The serial indirect effect was significant, effect = .026, 95% CI [.01, .04]. These findings suggest that perceived peer misconduct is associated with academic misconduct predisposition partly through higher moral disengagement and lower shame. The study provides a theory-consistent account of how perceived peer norms, moral rationalization, and affective self-sanctions are related to academic integrity among university students.

title: Nomophobia in the association between sport anxiety and happiness: Evidence from a cross-sectional mediation model.
abstract: This study examines the relationship between sport anxiety and happiness by focusing on the mediating role of nomophobia among university students. Grounded in the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping and Uses and Gratifications Theory, the study uses these theoretical perspectives only as conceptual frameworks for interpreting the observed statistical associations. The sample consists of 390 undergraduate students (48.2% female, 51.8% male; all participants were aged 18 years or older) enrolled in Faculties of Sport Sciences. Data were collected using the Sport Anxiety Scale-2 (SAS-2), the Nomophobia Scale (NMP-Q), and the Happiness Scale. Mediation analysis was conducted using Hayes PROCESS macro (Model 4) with 5,000 bootstrap samples to test indirect effects. The findings indicate that sport anxiety is significantly negatively associated with happiness while being positively associated with levels of nomophobia. In contrast, nomophobia shows a significant positive association with happiness. The mediation results reveal a significant indirect effect, indicating a competitive mediation pattern. Specifically, while sport anxiety is directly associated with lower levels of happiness, it is also indirectly associated with higher levels of happiness through higher nomophobia scores. These findings suggest that the observed statistical pattern may be compatible with a compensatory interpretation of nomophobia. However, because of the cross-sectional design, this interpretation should be regarded as a possible explanation rather than evidence of an underlying psychological process. The study contributes to the literature by highlighting the complexity of the statistical associations among sport anxiety, nomophobia, and happiness.

title: Associations of childhood body composition trajectories and adolescent body dissatisfaction: Longitudinal evidence from the UK Millennium Cohort Study.
abstract: Body dissatisfaction is common, particularly among those with higher BMIs. Issues with BMI as an adiposity measure may limit our understanding of how body weight is associated with body dissatisfaction, particularly given gendered body ideals. We investigated the association of childhood trajectories of BMI, fat mass index (FMI), and fat-free mass index (FFMI) with body dissatisfaction at age 14, and sex differences in these associations. This was a secondary analysis of UK Millennium Cohort Study data. Our exposures were trajectories of BMI (3-14 years), FMI and FFMI (7-14 years), modelled using latent class growth analysis. Our outcome was body dissatisfaction at 14 years. We used univariable and multivariable linear regression models to investigate associations and interaction terms to test for sex differences. Among 13,025 participants (49.2% female; 84.4% White), we found three BMI, FMI, and FFMI trajectories (low, moderate, high). Participants with moderate (adjusted mean difference [aMD] 0.32, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.24, 0.39) and high (aMD 0.71, 95% CI 0.55, 0.86) BMI trajectories and those with moderate (aMD 0.33, 95% CI 0.25, 0.41) and high (aMD 0.73, 95% CI 0.57, 0.89) FMI trajectories had higher body dissatisfaction scores than those with low trajectories. We did not find evidence that these associations differed by sex. For FFMI trajectories, boys with high (aMD 0.31, 95% CI 0.17, 0.46), but not moderate (aMD 0.07, 95% CI -0.03, 0.17) trajectories had greater body dissatisfaction. In girls, mean differences by FFMI trajectory were consistent with adiposity results. BMI and FMI trajectories are similarly associated with body dissatisfaction when FMI is estimated using bioelectrical impedance analysis. Both boys and girls may be susceptible to weight-related body dissatisfaction in adolescence. Further research is needed to understand how muscularity is associated with body dissatisfaction.

title: Automating Observable Closure Analysis for Graph Transformation Models with MolFoundry
abstract: Graph transformations model changing systems, with applications in software, biology and chemistry, among others. We introduce MolFoundry, a graph transformation framework, and present a workflow for observable analysis that tracks the dynamics of local patterns through rule composition. Analysing rule compositions avoids the need to enumerate a potentially infinite state space. Building on rule-algebraic stochastic rewriting, MolFoundry's kernel composes rules with nested application conditions, including missing-edge constraints. Given rules, rates and query patterns, the algorithms iteratively identify auxiliary pattern counts and search for closure. Using exact counting identities supplied by graph-family backends, successful searches yield closed ordinary differential equations for average counts or, with justified individual jumps, finite event models describing joint changes and rates. We evaluate conditional composition and automated discovery of auxiliary observables against published calculations and independent rule application. Applications to aldol addition, copolymerization and chlorination show how the framework yields quantitative predictions directly from molecular graph rules.
comment: 30 pages, including appendices. Software: https://github.com/dmerkle/molfoundry-observables . Interactive examples and executable notebooks: https://stochmech.algochem.techfak.de/

title: Separating mixtures of single-fiber orientation distributions for increased sensitivity to crossing white matter fibers
abstract: Intro: Diffusion MRI allows for in vivo probing of brain tissue architecture via micron-level diffusion aggregated at the millimeter scale, but crossing white matter fibers decrease the sensitivity of downstream tasks such as microstructural modeling and tractography. Current fixel-based methods for identifying the number, orientation, and spread of fibers rely on finding the peaks of fiber orientation distributions from constrained spherical deconvolution. However, this method is biased by the spreads of nearby fibers and fails at angular separations lower than approximately 40-50 degrees. Methods: In this work, we perform a constrained nonlinear optimization called fiber segmentation by signal splitting and iterative least squares estimation (FISSILE), modeling each voxel as a mixture of single-fiber distributions. We use FISSILE to fit axially symmetric fibers in simulations and on three in vivo human subjects from the Human Connectome Project, an ex vivo raccoon brain, as well as the same human subject scanned twice at two different signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs). Results: On simulated data, FISSILE successfully identifies fibers at an angular separation of 40° and a volume fraction of 0.1 at an SNR as low as 30, while MRtrix3's fod2fixel is limited to 60° separation and 0.1 volume fraction at the same SNR. On acquired data, FISSILE identified 85.8% of white matter voxels on average in human brains and 79.4% in the raccoon with at least one fiber crossing, whereas fod2fixel identified 30.1% and 44.5%. The number of white matter fiber crossings was mildly sensitive to different noise levels in the human subject with two acquisitions. Conclusion: A method that models the crossing fiber phenomenon as an unmixing problem increases sensitivity to individual fibers for more precise characterization of anatomy.

title: How large an effect would we have seen? Positive controls, detection floors and dataset pitfalls in scalp-EEG speech decoding
abstract: Objective. Studies that decode imagined speech from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) commonly validate their pipelines with a positive control, usually overt speech, and report null results without stating what effect size the pipeline could have detected. Approach. Using ds003626 ("Thinking out loud"), KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, we audited decoding of overt speech, articulator preparation and imagined speech with artifact-channel subsets, band-limited decoding and trial selection, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion. We injected class-dependent effects of known amplitude into the real recordings to measure the detection floor of five decoder families, and we checked the ds003626 labels against the dataset's acquisition protocol. Main results. On ds003626, two lip electrodes decoded overt speech at 0.7430 and the eight external channels at 0.7068, against 0.4231 for the 128-channel scalp montage, and no decodable signal survived in the 8-30 Hz band. On the other two corpora, within-subject accuracy rose monotonically with frequency into the range dominated by muscle activity. Band-power logistic regression detected an injected 8-30 Hz desynchronization of 0.54 uV under a criterion fixed in advance, whereas a compact convolutional network (EEGNet) detected nothing within subject up to 4.31 uV. In ds003626, the condition codes are the reverse of the intuitive reading, the class encoding changed between public releases, and condition is a deterministic function of time within each session. Significance. In these corpora the overt-speech positive control is dominated by myogenic signal and cannot validate a decoding pipeline. We recommend that speech-decoding studies report band-limited and artifact-channel accuracy, the direction of accuracy across frequency, and a measured detection floor.
comment: 22 pages, 4 figures, 8 tables plus supplementary tables. To be submitted to Journal of Neural Engineering

title: Predicting Unseen Scientific Interactions: Conditional Flow Models Hallucinate Non-Additive Effects
abstract: Conditional generative models are increasingly used for scientific prediction beyond the direct training support. Yet scientific questions often concern whether one intervention changes the effect of another. Such interactions can be of primary interest while explaining little of the total variation, allowing models to appear accurate overall without recovering the relevant scientific effect. It remains unclear how these models learn interactions and when these successfully extrapolate to unseen conditions. We therefore study interaction recovery in flow-matching models using a physiological time-series simulator, drug dose-response data, combinatorial cell perturbations, and molecular conformer generations, where we separate recovery from hallucinated interaction structure. In the controlled setting, individual effects are learned much earlier than interactions and models hallucinate interactions where none exist. Across settings, we find qualitatively different generalization problems, with successful prediction depending on whether condition structure continues from observed to held-out targets. When it does, interactions are recoverable. If not, models can generate plausible responses while missing the interaction. We furthermore find that hallucinations increase as targets become less identifiable, and that successful interaction recovery in output space can fail under nonlinear readouts. Finally, we show that aggregate fidelity metrics can conceal whether models learn and extrapolate interactions.
comment: Accepted as an oral at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: AI Data Readiness for Scientific Discovery (AIDaR). Code: https://github.com/SamGijsen/interaction-flows

title: Feasibility of a Patient-Specific Digital Twin for Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt Trajectory Planning
abstract: Catheter obstruction is the commonest cause of shunt failure; freehand insertion at Keen's point leaves the tip free in cerebrospinal fluid in only one case in ten. We built a digital twin that reconstructs skull, scalp, ear and ventricles from preoperative CT by deterministic geometry, searches every entry around Keen's point for the perpendicular trajectory with the longest intraventricular length under safety constraints, and returns the plan as two ruler measurements from the ear and two depths. Executed freehand in 11 consecutive adults (IDEAL Stage 2a), it achieved Hayhurst Grade 1 placement in 10 of 11 against 22 of 213 historically (p = 9 x 10^-9), median entry and angular deviations 2.5 mm and 5.9 degrees, 1.4 cm more intraventricular catheter than Keen's point, and no intraoperative complication. The technique was unchanged; the gain came from choosing entry and depth per patient. Whether it lowers revision is the next stage's hypothesis.
comment: 29 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables; includes Supplementary Information

title: Maximum likelihood, neural networks and posterior mean for inferring fractional Brownian motion parameters
abstract: Fractional Brownian motion (fBM) is a model of anomalous diffusion parameterised by a Hurst exponent $H \in (0,1)$ and a generalised diffusion coefficient $D_H > 0$. We jointly estimate $H$ and $D_H$ using maximum likelihood (MLE) from density measurements with Poisson counting noise and single-particle trajectory with Gaussian localisation error. We show that one density measurement in time cannot infer both $H$ and $D_H$ and that several time points are needed, which matters most for inference precision. For trajectories, we show that a neural network trained with a squared error loss approximates the posterior mean of $H$, which can be computed exactly at negligible cost. Paired with the profile-likelihood estimate of $D_H$, the posterior mean has the lowest root mean squared error in both $H$ and $D_H$, except near $H=0$ and $H=1$ where MLE estimates $H$ better. In vesicle trajectories from two cell types, $H$ and $D_H$ form a continuum rather than distinct modes of motion. The posterior probability that each window within a track is subdiffusive or superdiffusive shows that $26\%$ of MRC5 fibroblast and $21\%$ of HeLa vesicle trajectories contain both subdiffusive and superdiffusive windows, against $2\%$ and $7\%$ expected from estimation uncertainty alone. Intracellular cargoes therefore switch between subdiffusion and superdiffusion over time rather than forming populations with fixed $H$.

title: ProtModernBERT: Compute-Efficient Protein Language Modeling
abstract: Large protein language models provide a powerful framework for learning sequence-function relationships and guiding experimental design. However, architectural improvements are underexplored, especially in low-compute regimes of relevance for resource-constrained research laboratories. We show that the training cost for encoder-only transformer architectures can be reduced by leveraging modern architectural refinements, offering an encouraging performance / compute-efficiency trade-off. We introduce ProtModernBERT, a modernized BERT-style model pre-trained on amino acid sequences, and compare it with ProtBert, Amplify, and ESM2 across a set of supervised structural tasks -encompassing secondary structure prediction, disorder prediction, and subcellular localization- and ProteinGym's zero-shot functional benchmark. We find that ProtModernBERT matches or closely tracks the performance of Amplify-120M and ProtBert with up to 80-90\% reduction in pre-training FLOPs, and narrows the gap to ESM2 when controlling for pre-training. Our analysis using a cluster-based validation protocol for hyperparameter selection and randomly initialized models disentangles the contributions of architecture and data, showing that modern components provide stronger inductive biases that are more consequential than parameter count in low-compute regimes.

title: Structure Before Intelligence: Gating What Agentic Scientific Workflows Release
abstract: An agentic scientific workflow can run to completion and still release wrong results: a silent numerical error, a stale input, or a defect in a shared upstream step can contaminate several outputs while a sibling branch stays correct. We treat trust in such results as a release decision. A harness around the workflow's directed acyclic graph (DAG) decides which outputs may be used: it enforces mandatory checks, contains failures to the affected branch, recomputes from tracked versions, adds validators, and releases a result only if a risk model estimates its probability of being invalid as low. Language-model agents work inside the harness, choosing corrective actions and reviewing releases, but cannot override it. On 60 held-out paired instances of two workflows with injected faults, we switched components on and off. Each supplied a different property. Containment and recovery raised the number of correct results. Validation supplied safety: fixed rules without validation released 37 invalid results, while validating every candidate released none. Risk estimation supplied efficiency, matching that safety with 31% fewer validators at somewhat lower yield, although better targeting than random validation was not shown. Lineage evidence helped on one workflow. The language model added no measurable benefit: whether invalid results escaped depended on the harness, not the model. This proof of concept points to a practical path: placing agents inside explicit release-control structure can keep released scientific results trustworthy, and it gives more capable agents a measurable baseline to improve on.
comment: 21 pages: 10-page main paper and 11-page supplement; 2 figures

title: Statistical Mechanics of Spike Trains: Self-Consistent Activity Ensembles and Phase Transitions
abstract: We introduce a statistical-mechanical framework for spiking neuronal systems in which entire spike trains, defined as spatiotemporal configurations of discrete events, are treated as microstates of the system. Instead of modeling explicit network dynamics, we construct an ensemble over complete spike histories and assign to each configuration an effective energy functional that quantifies its consistency with intrinsic synaptic interactions. This formulation leads to a Boltzmann-like distribution over spike configurations, where an effective temperature captures the influence of external inputs acting as a stochastic drive. Macroscopic states are described in terms of coarse-grained observables, such as population firing-rate densities, and arise from a competition between energetic contributions favoring interaction-consistent spike patterns and entropic contributions favoring spatio-temporal disorder. Within this framework, we primarily characterize the transition between oscillatory and non-oscillatory activity. The non-oscillatory regime contains both broadly distributed, approximately uniform states and temporally localized collapsed states, whereas the oscillatory regime is characterized by repeated activity peaks. These regimes are diagnosed using order parameters derived from the population spike-rate density, including its entropy, temporal localization measures, and autocorrelation-based indicators. To complement the analytical treatment, we perform Monte Carlo simulations that sample the ensemble of admissible spike configurations using a Metropolis-Hastings scheme defined directly on spike trains. The simulations reveal the emergence of the predicted macroscopic regimes and provide a direct sampling-based probe of the free-energy landscape.

title: Cross-subject decoding of imagined speech from scalp EEG: a leakage-controlled evaluation on three public corpora
abstract: Objective. A decoder of imagined speech that works for a new user without calibration would make a non-invasive speech interface practical. We tested whether imagined-speech content recorded with scalp electroencephalography (EEG) transfers across people, and examined why accuracy within a single person remains low. Approach. We analyzed three public corpora, ds003626, KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion and reports exact binomial thresholds, group tests and bootstrap confidence intervals. We trained decoders on each participant and tested them on every other, compared representational geometry across participants without a classifier, applied subject-level alignment, and tested five explanations for the within-subject ceiling. Main results. Across 482 ordered pairs of participants, no pair survived correction for multiple comparisons; mean pair-transfer accuracy lay within 0.006 of chance on every corpus, while every within-subject reference lay above it. Imagery against pre-stimulus rest generalized at about 0.61 after artifact and elapsed-time controls, but its decoder labelled the interval preceding imagery as imagery as often as imagery itself, so the contrast reflects a post-stimulus state, not imagery. Within subject, only the competition corpus decoded above threshold for every participant (0.3147; chance 0.200); syllable count explained little of this, but its frequency profile failed an artifact audit. Significance. In these corpora, imagined-speech content did not transfer between people through any representation we examined. Trial count per class was the only variable that ordered the corpora, which favors larger single-condition datasets over further model development.
comment: 23 pages, 5 figures, 10 tables plus supplementary tables. To be submitted to Journal of Neural Engineering

title: Awakening as a Trait-Level Transformation of Consciousness
abstract: Awakening is reported across contemplative traditions yet remains poorly defined in science, where it is often conflated with transient states induced by meditation or psychedelics, obscuring its significance for theories of consciousness and cognitive architecture. We treat awakening as a functional construct capturing convergence across Hindu and Buddhist sources, phenomenological and psychometric findings, and neuroimaging evidence. Synthesizing these literatures, we find convergent evidence for reorganization across dimensions including self-related processing, affective reactivity, and temporal structure, while exposing limits of paradigms for detecting trait-level change. We argue that awakening is best understood not as a transient state but as a trait-level reorganization of experience, centered on a reduction in identification with mental contents rather than the acquisition of new content. To account for this contentless transformation, we propose the enactive-dereification model (EDM), which treats training and awakening as graded differences along a dereification gradient, from a reified to a relational mode of experience. We offer an operational definition that distinguishes awakening from state-dependent experiences and psychopathology, emphasizing dynamical flexibility and stabilization of a dereified mode. The framework yields falsifiable predictions linking independently assessed trait transformation to large-scale neural dynamics and provides a basis for distinguishing adaptive contemplative change from pathological ego-dissolution.

title: Two dissociable axes of brain hierarchical dynamics track universal and population-specific effects of mindfulness
abstract: How mental training reshapes the temporal architecture of large-scale brain dynamics and how these mechanisms differ between healthy and clinically vulnerable populations remains poorly understood. Time-averaged neural measures collapse the multi-scale nature of brain activity, obscuring the dynamic processes through which behavioural interventions reorganise hierarchical brain function. Here, applying a sliding-window Temporal Irreversibility Index to source-reconstructed EEG across three complementary cohorts (n = 141), we decompose hierarchical brain trajectories into three orthogonal temporal descriptors and uncover two dissociable, mechanistically interpretable axes of intervention-induced plasticity. Cumulative meditation practice drives a universal, pan-cerebral reduction in the exploratory breadth of hierarchical dynamics, tracking dose-dependently with lifetime hours of practice. Temporal persistence is bidirectionally tuned by 8-week mindfulness-based interventions in a population-specific way: reduced in healthy meditators but increased in trauma-exposed individuals, revealing that comparable MBI protocols engage qualitatively distinct network mechanisms depending on baseline clinical status. A joint Hidden Markov Model further links these dynamical shifts to distinct microstate substrates, and longitudinal changes selectively track improvements in a single facet of mindfulness, attentional presence in daily life. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for how behavioural training reorganises non-equilibrium brain dynamics, with direct implications for tailoring mindfulness-based interventions to individual clinical profiles.

title: Semantic Alignment of EEG and Text: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Decoding Imagined Speech
abstract: Imagined speech decoding from EEG offers a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces. Traditional closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not explicitly exploit relationships among linguistic intents, limiting output flexibility. We adapt a multimodal contrastive learning framework to imagined speech, aligning EEG trials with language representations in the embedding space of a frozen pretrained text encoder. An EEG encoder is trained with a composite objective combining semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination, encouraging semantic structure while preserving separability among 39 intent categories. We evaluate the approach on the Chisco imagined speech dataset across five subjects, reporting Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy (2v2). We also investigate maximum EEG-text cosine similarity (MaxCosine) as an intrinsic indicator of decoding reliability and probe semantic structure beyond category labels using five evaluation-time semantic axes and a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe (SGP) with previously unseen candidate sentences. The contrastive framework achieved decoding performance comparable to a task-optimized closed-set classifier while mapping EEG into a frozen language embedding space. MaxCosine identified subsets of held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy across subjects. Evaluation-time semantic axes showed mean agreement above the 50% chance reference across all five dimensions, and the SGP qualitatively illustrated direct comparison with unseen candidate sentences. Together, these findings suggest that EEG-language alignment can retain comparable fixed-intent decoding while supporting similarity-based retrieval, intrinsic reliability ranking, and evaluation of broader semantic structure.

title: EEG Correlates of Verbal and Perceptual Reasoning
abstract: Identifying the neural underpinnings of intelligence is one of the major goals of modern intelligence research. However, few imaging studies explore the high extremes of intelligence, and most use only a single composite IQ score. This study used quantitative EEG recordings to investigate correlations between the EEG variables of individual alpha peak frequency, relative power, and coherence, and scores on verbal and perceptual reasoning tests in participants with IQs from the low-average to exceptionally gifted ranges. Overall, the results did not reveal any pattern of significant relationships between these EEG measures and the two psychometric tests. Since this study had only a small sample, heavily skewed towards the high-IQ end of the scale, no definitive conclusions about the EEG measures and verbal and perceptual reasoning can be drawn. Nevertheless, it reveals many opportunities for further research, and suggestions are made for progressing this topic in the future.

title: Reciprocity coordinates a three-way trade-off in recurrent neural circuits
abstract: Biological neural circuits contain both unidirectional and reciprocal connections, but how reciprocity affects circuit computation remains unclear. We varied reciprocity \r{ho} across 21 levels in recurrent-network simulations while holding network size, connection density, and directed-edge count fixed. Low-reciprocity networks produced more diverse stimulus-driven activity and performed better on four continuous-input tasks, whereas higher reciprocity generally improved performance on three delayed-memory tasks. Increasing reciprocity reduced online memory capacity and accelerated recovery from perturbations. A post-cue noise experiment showed that higher reciprocity suppressed internal noise propagation but made cue-evoked states less distinguishable, and component matching separated the contributions of cue separation and within-cue dispersion to readout robustness. Within this ensemble, reciprocity thus mediates a three-way trade-off among representational capacity, local stability, and task-state separability: higher reciprocity lowers capacity, strengthens stability, and compresses separability. Whether it improves behaviour depends on whether the stability gain outweighs the lost separation between task states. Connectome and microcircuit datasets from five species showed intermediate reciprocity, while reciprocity varied substantially across adult Drosophila brain regions, providing compatible structural context and motivating circuit-specific functional tests.

title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
abstract: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

title: Platelet-driven contraction enlarges accessible space in layered fibrin networks without uniformly accelerating particle escape
abstract: Platelet traction contracts fibrin networks, yet whether contraction promotes or hinders the escape of suspended particles is unclear. We coupled an overdamped Langevin model of platelet--fibrin mechanics to Brownian transport of finite-size tracers through frozen network states. Nine mechanical replicas were evolved at four filopodial traction baselines (0--8.8\,nN), stacked into 5-$μ$m-thick domains of 50 layers and probed at 0--15\,s with 0.5-$μ$m tracers (29,952 trajectories, 100\,s observation). Benchmarked against experimental clot-contraction kinetics, the simulated contraction is post-lag, within one order of magnitude of experimental rates and corresponds to the onset of the contraction phase. Relative to the matched zero-baseline control, every active-baseline state showed greater projected contraction and a larger tracer-accessible volume ($+9.3\%$ to $+27.6\%$; exact sign test $p=0.0039$ per condition). At 15\,s, mean survival at 100\,s fell from 27.3\% to 14.3\% and the restricted mean exit time from 56.5 to 44.0\,s between the lowest and highest baseline, and all nine replicas shortened residence at 8.8\,nN. At lower baselines, responses differed among replicas, and nearly all retained tracers with a classified start were connected to an exit. Contraction therefore enlarges accessible space without uniformly accelerating escape, separating geometric accommodation from transport kinetics.

title: Maternal experience unmasks temporal integration for vocalization processing
abstract: New parents become highly responsive to infant cries in parallel with auditory cortical plasticity enhancing representations of these calls. To promote caretaking behavior, increased cortical activity must be appropriately routed to downstream areas in combination with suppression of circuits that could promote aversive responses to infant cries. We investigated responses to multi syllable mouse pup calls in cortical output neurons projecting to either the auditory striatum or auditory midbrain (inferior colliculus) using longitudinal 2-photon imaging and in vivo optically tagged whole-cell recordings. In mice with maternal experience, corticocollicular but not corticostriatal projections responded to pup calls over extended durations and were required for pup retrieval behavior, indicating that corticocollicular output neurons integrated multiple call syllables. The two populations diverged with parental experience, enhancing sustained responses in corticocollicular projections and reducing responses in corticostriatal projections. We performed simultaneous Neuropixels recordings from auditory cortex, thalamus, and midbrain to examine the temporal structure of call responses across areas, and to determine the influences of feedforward and feedback processing. Facilitation of later syllables increased in midbrain of maternally experienced animals, together with reduced firing rates in a subset of units that were weakly coupled to cortical and midbrain activity. Overall, maternal experience leads to broad suppression of subcortical excitation in response to pup calls while selectively unmasking a subset of midbrain neurons that integrate over multiple syllables.

title: Whole-brain neural substrates of behavioral variability in the larval zebrafish
abstract: Animals engaged in naturalistic behavior can exhibit a large degree of behavioral variability even under sensory invariant conditions. Such behavioral variability can include not only variations of the same behavior, but also variability across qualitatively different behaviors driven by divergent cognitive states, such as fight-or-flight decisions. However, the neural circuit mechanisms that generate such divergent behaviors across trials are not well understood. To investigate this question, here we studied the visual-evoked responses of larval zebrafish to moving objects of various sizes, which we found exhibited highly variable and divergent responses across repetitions of the same stimulus. Given that the neuronal circuits underlying such behaviors span sensory, motor, and other brain areas, we built a novel Fourier light field microscope which enables high-resolution, volumetric imaging across the larval zebrafish during behavior. This enabled us to screen for neural loci which exhibited activity patterns correlated with behavioral variability. We found that despite the highly variable activity of neurons, visual stimuli were robustly encoded at the population level, and the visual-encoding dimensions of neural activity did not explain behavioral variability. This robustness despite apparent neuronal variability was due to the multi-dimensional geometry of the neuronal population dynamics: almost all neural dimensions that were variable across individual trials, i.e. the noise modes, were nearly orthogonal to those encoding for sensory information. Investigating this neuronal variability further, we identified two sparsely-distributed, brain-wide neuronal populations whose pre-motor activity predicted whether the larva would respond to a stimulus and, if so, which direction it would turn on a single-trial level. These populations predicted single-trial behavior seconds before stimulus onset, indicating they encoded time-varying internal states modulating behavior, perhaps organizing behavior over longer timescales or enabling flexible behavior routines. Our results provide the first brain-wide evidence that sensory, motor, and internal variables are represented in a highly mixed fashion across widely distributed neuronal populations and demonstrate that de-mixing each of these components at the neuronal population level is critical to understanding the mechanisms underlying the brain's remarkable flexibility and robustness.

title: Rapid Emergence of an Adaptive Spatial Representation
abstract: Peripheral sensory cue availability fluctuates across timescales ranging from seconds to years. This requires central circuits to continuously adapt their representations while preserving established codes, but how the brain achieves this flexibility is unknown. Using two-photon calcium imaging in the mouse inferior colliculus, we address this knowledge gap by testing how neurons encode sound location before and after abruptly disrupting binaural cues via monaural hearing loss. Despite measurable single neuron changes, altering binaural cues had remarkably little impact on the encoding of auditory space. Rather, neural activity rotated into a spatially informative representational subspace, orthogonal to the original binaural axis, within two hours of hearing loss. This rotation occurred in absence of overt experience or training, and reflected a shift from ON- to OFF-dominated spatial selectivity. Thus, central population codes rapidly reorganize to accommodate sudden changes at the periphery, without overwriting existing representations.

title: Spanning spatial scales with functional imaging in the human brain; initial experiences at 10.5 Tesla
abstract: One of the most important new frontiers in the effort to improve the spatial resolution and accuracy of imaging of human brain activity is the recent development of greater than 10 Tesla magnetic fields. Here we present initial results for 10.5 Tesla Blood Oxygenation Level Dependent (BOLD) based functional brain imaging (fMRI) of the human brain acquired with previously unavailable or difficult to attain spatial resolutions and functional contrast. We present data obtained with nominal isotropic resolutions ranging from 0.65 to 0.35 mm for partial brain coverage for stimulus evoked responses, and 0.75 mm for whole brain coverage to capture the spontaneous fluctuations that are the source of functional connectivity measures. The increasingly higher nominal resolutions (i.e. smaller voxel volumes and dimensions) employed in image acquisition were shown to correspond to real gains in resolution using image reconstruction methods developed to minimize blurring. Existence of supralinear gains in stimulus-evoked percent signal change and major improvements in statistical significance were evident relative to 7 Tesla, the most advanced commercially available ultrahigh magnetic field platform currently employed in human brain studies. These results were feasible due to gains in intrinsic signal-to-noise ratio, BOLD contrast, and image acceleration provided by the uniquely high magnetic field of 10.5 Tesla, and the use of novel high channel count arrays to capture these gains. The results provide a preview of the potential that will be available in the new era of greater than 10 Tesla human functional imaging, particularly for mesoscale functional organizations and connectivity.

title: Targeted preoptic neuronal activation induces a hypothermic state with metabolic reprogramming and acute cerebroprotection
abstract: Therapeutic hypothermia is cerebroprotective in experimental stroke but has shown limited clinical efficacy due to metabolically costly counter regulatory responses. Naturally occurring states such as torpor achieve hypothermia through coordinated regulation of temperature and metabolism are associated with cerebroprotection. Here, we tested whether selective activation of a genetically defined thermoregulatory neuronal population is sufficient to induce hypothermia after ischemic injury and whether temperature-dependent cerebroprotection is accompanied by metabolic remodeling. Using chemogenetic tools, kappa opioid receptor expressing neurons in the preoptic area were activated in mice subjected to transient middle cerebral artery occlusion. Core body temperature, metabolism, infarct volume, and motor recovery were assessed under conditions permitting hypothermia or maintaining normothermia. Untargeted metabolomic profiling was performed on whole brain tissue collected 30 minutes after activation in the absence of ischemia. Activation of kappa opioid receptor expressing preoptic neurons induced a hypothermic state with coordinated metabolic changes, reduced infarct volume and improved acute motor outcomes. These effects were attenuated when body temperature was maintained at normothermia. Metabolomic profiling revealed coordinated alterations in nucleotide, phospholipid, and sphingolipid pathways. These findings link temperature dependent cerebroprotection to coordinated metabolic remodeling, with translational relevance for stroke.

title: Grid cells are not a parsimonious source of the hexadirectional signal
abstract: Hexadirectional modulation is widely treated as a proxy for population-level grid-cell activity in humans. Conventional analyses test the sixth harmonic of the mean directional response, whereas we show grid-cell firing predicts a dominant sixfold modulation of cell-level variance, rather than population-level mean. Using analytical derivations, simulations and recordings from 23,453 rodent medial entorhinal neurons, we show that grid cell tuning alone cannot account for the measured mean signal. Analysis of 1,349 conjunctive grid-head-direction cells revealed insufficient grid-axis alignment and directional tuning specificity to account for population-level hexadirectionality. A hypothetical additional nonlinearity mechanism near the cell level can produce a a small sixfold population-level mean modulation, [≤] 2%, under favorable circumstances. Moreover, the current methodology does not adequately differentiate genuinely symmetric activity and stable directional peaks, nor contextualize a harmonic measurement in a solid spectral framework. These findings show that mean hexadirectional modulation neither follows directly from grid-cell firing nor uniquely identifies grid-cell activity. We provide an improved framework for testing a link between the two in future studies.

title: HERO: A hierarchy-aware analysis pipeline for reducing and refining whole-brain atlas-mapped cellular datasets
abstract: Advances in high-throughput mesoscale microscopy and machine learning-based image analysis pipelines have made unbiased whole-brain imaging widely accessible. However, translating the resulting atlas-mapped datasets into biologically meaningful results remains a substantial barrier owing to their sheer magnitude and complex hierarchical organization. Consequently, reporting structure and analysis methods vary widely across studies, undermining rigor and reproducibility. To address this, we developed a user-friendly data reduction workflow, HERO (Hierarchy-aware Expression Region Organization), designed to perform hierarchy-aware selection, refinement, ranking, and visualization of whole-brain cell detection datasets. The workflow is customizable to specific needs, requires minimal coding experience, and outputs transparent, curated results. HERO functions as a seamless plug-in within larger-scale whole-brain cell detection analysis pipelines, providing efficient, unbiased region selection to streamline subsequent statistical analyses and comparative evaluations. Although HERO is developed with mouse cell-detection datasets, it can be applied to any atlas-mapped dataset that contains hierarchical information. Here, we applied the HERO pipeline to example cell detection datasets containing afferent cells from the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and the insular cortex (insula). HERO provided top projecting regions consistent with historical tracing studies for the BST (e.g., amygdalar and hypothalamic regions) and the insula (e.g., somatosensory, autonomic, and interoceptive regions). Furthermore, the refinement step of HERO provides additional enriched regions originally obscured in the primary ranked outputs, such as memory- and emotion-associated structures. With HEROs dynamic processing, we were able to identify top-projecting regions consistent with the literature and, additionally, find regions often obscured in these large datasets. In sum, HERO offers a standardized analysis workflow to reduce whole-brain cell-detection datasets, transforming raw regional cell counts into curated results and advancing the effectiveness, interpretability, and accessibility of whole-brain imaging in neuroscience.

title: Postprandial hypertriglyceridemia activates microglia to promote satiety via an ASC dependent signaling.
abstract: Reactive microglia are commonly considered neurotoxic and detrimental for brain functioning. Chronic consumption of a high-fat diet strongly activates microglia, disrupts the central control of energy metabolism, contributes to obesity, and promotes cognitive decline. In this study we report an unexpected beneficial function of microglia reaction at the time scale of a meal, whereby they promote satiety in a macronutrient-dependent manner. We show that murine microglia react to ingested dietary fat within three hours. Specifically, postprandial hypertriglyceridemia induced microglial hyper-ramification alongside with a transcriptional reprogramming promoting communication with neurons. This effect occurs in discrete brain areas, including the hypothalamus and the brainstem, which control hunger. Remarkably, microglia-specific genetic ablation of Apoptosis-associated Speck-like protein containing a CARD (named ASC), a master regulator of metabolism, immune function and cell shape, profoundly alters satiety following high-fat food consumption. These results reveal that microglia engage an immune signaling pathway to rapidly alert the neural circuits and activate an anorectic response that limits overconsumption of dietary fat. Unexpectedly, this regulatory process is sexually dimorphic, present in males only. Furthermore, we found that the postprandial microglial reaction is bypassed during obesity, providing a new therapeutic target to treat maladaptive eating disorders.

title: Neural Representations of Visual Anagrams in Macaque Inferotemporal Cortex
abstract: Visual recognition requires stable representations of object identity despite large changes in the retinal image. Yet this stability must be selective: some transformations change not only how an image looks, but also what object it appears to depict. Visual anagrams highlight this challenge: a single image can resemble two different objects at different orientations, such as an elephant and a rabbit. Here, we asked how macaque inferotemporal (IT) cortex represents such transformations. We recorded large neuronal populations while presenting visual anagrams and unambiguous exemplars of their two interpretations across rotations. Neurons preferring one exemplar tended to prefer anagram orientations supporting the corresponding interpretation. At each of the two interpretation-relevant canonical angles, population responses more closely resembled those to the matching exemplar than those to the nonmatching exemplar. This matching advantage persisted when both exemplars were presented at the alternative canonical angle. Decoders trained exclusively on exemplars across rotations also tracked the shifts in anagram representations. Visual models showed anagram-exemplar alignment as well, with stronger alignment in models with greater relative shape preference. These findings suggest that transformation tolerance in IT is sensitive to what an image appears to depict, while relative shape preference is associated with similar representational organization in visual models.

title: Reaching movements in virtual reality depend on the seen avatar arm and not just the acting arm
abstract: Virtual reality (VR) offers unique opportunities to study behaviour by allowing the visual environment to be manipulated in ways otherwise impossible in the real world. A central theoretical question is how body-related visual information shapes movement control. Given right-handers' greater dexterity with the right arm, perhaps even seeing a right arm vs. a left arm may engage sensorimotor processes associated with more precise motor control. We examined reaching performance while participants used their own right or left arm to move the manipulandum of a KINARM robot to intercept static targets. Participants wore a VR head-mounted display, calibrated to the robot's physical workspace, in which they saw either the right or left arm holding and moving the manipulandum. The 2 x 2 design allowed for independent manipulation of the controlling arm and virtual arm displayed. As expected, reaches were faster and more accurate when controlled by the right arm. More interestingly, performance was also affected by the seen arm. Participants made straighter reaches when they saw a virtual right arm than a left arm, especially for the right controlling arm. These findings show that precise motor control relies not only on the arm that is actually moved and provides proprioceptive feedback, but also on the visual identity of the arm. The ability to modulate performance using visual features in VR opens new theoretical questions and opportunities for applications such as rehabilitation.

title: Recovering Hidden Neural Oscillatory Modes from Partial Observations through Delay Embedding and Perturbation
abstract: Characterising the oscillatory behaviour generated by neural interactions is central to systems neuroscience because these dynamical properties are linked to brain function. However, inferring latent neural dynamics is challenging because recordings sample only part of the system. Time-delay embedding allows dynamical modes to be estimated from partial recordings, using methods such as Hankel dynamic mode decomposition (Hankel DMD). Despite its promise, two questions remain: what dynamical information is recoverable through time-delay embedding, and how can recovery be improved? We address both questions using control theory. Our framework centres on factorising the Hankel matrix of delay-embedded observations into an observability matrix and a trajectory matrix with the form of a controllability matrix. We show that their ranks impose complementary constraints on what any delay-embedding method can recover: delay embedding can increase observability rank, while perturbation can increase trajectory rank by exciting otherwise inactive modes. We validate this framework using Hankel DMD in simulations and human electrocorticography (ECoG). In both, perturbation increased the number of fast-decaying mode estimates, whereas greater delay depth increased the number of reliably estimated modes and, in ECoG, extended their frequency range. These results clarify what partial recordings can reveal about neural dynamics and how to reveal more.

title: A Reproducible Cortical Model of Focal Epileptiform Activity with a Multi-Biomarker Analysis Pipeline
abstract: The development of surface-based therapeutic strategies, including extracranial illumination and epicortical electrical or optoelectronic neuromodulation, requires experimental models in which focal pathological activity can be generated and monitored within an accessible cortical region. Here, we established an acute cortical model of focal epileptiform activity in anesthetized mice based on local microinjection of 4-aminopyridine (4-AP) into the barrel cortex. This preparation provides precise spatial and temporal control of the epileptiform focus while enabling simultaneous electrophysiological sampling across cortical depth. To objectively characterize the induced activity, we implemented a Python-based analysis pipeline integrating complementary electrophysiological biomarkers, including oscillatory power, multi-unit activity, pathological fast ripples (250-650 Hz), and epileptiform bursts. Local 4-AP administration produced robust increases in gamma (30-100 Hz) power, multi-unit firing (MUA), fast ripple and burst activity. Pharmacological sensitivity of the framework was evaluated using carbamazepine, which robustly attenuated 4-AP-induced increases in all biomarkers. Together, this study provides a reproducible experimental and analytical framework for investigating focal cortical epileptiform activity and for the future evaluation of pharmacological, optical, and electrical interventions targeting superficial cortical networks.

title: Predicting the Efficacy of Myopia Control Spectacle Lenses by Simulating Their Optical Effect on the Retina
abstract: Slowing myopia progression is central to addressing a growing public health concern. Myopia control spectacle lenses with diverse optical designs have been proposed for this purpose, and show varying degrees of clinical efficacy. Relating their design to their efficacy remains an open challenge. Here we show that it is possible to predict their clinical efficacy from their optical design, by reconstructing their impact on the retinal image. We simulated how several lens designs affect the retinal image using a combined lens and eye optical model. By assuming that the retina extracts specific features from the retinal image to modulate eye growth, we could predict the cumulative absolute reduction in axial elongation (CARE) of lens designs with very different rationales and microstructures. Our results show that different myopia control spectacle lenses can be compared on a common optical basis, and that their efficacy is predictable from their optical properties. This work paves the way for rational design of next-generation lenses and for adapting designs to each patient's ocular optics.

title: Dizocilpine-derived K2060 exhibits enhanced blockage at NMDA receptors with impaired Mg2+ block and provides strong protection against audiogenic seizures
abstract: Background and Purpose: Voltage-dependent Mg2+ block is a defining feature of the GluN1/GluN2 subtype of N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs). We tested how impaired Mg2+ block at GluN1/GluN2A receptors mutated at the GluN2A-N615 position modifies inhibition by dizocilpine-derived K2060 compared with clinically used memantine and ketamine. Experimental Approach: Electrophysiological recordings were performed on recombinant wild-type (WT) and mutated GluN1/GluN2A receptors expressed in HEK293T cells. Acute hippocampal slice electrophysiology and behavioural studies were conducted in WT and knock-in GluN2A-N615S mice. In vivo tolerability and efficacy were evaluated using open field testing, prepulse inhibition (PPI), and protection against audiogenic seizures (AGS). Key Results: Mg2+ reduced the apparent potency of all three blockers and slowed onset at the GluN1/GluN2A-WT receptor. These Mg2+-dependent effects were absent or markedly reduced at the GluN1/GluN2A-N615S and GluN1/GluN2A-N615K receptors. In addition, K2060 showed slower unbinding and greater trapping than memantine. In hippocampal slices from GluN2A-N615S mice, K2060 exhibited enhanced but slower onset inhibition than memantine and ketamine. In vivo, K2060 caused no overt behavioural disruption at 5 mg/kg (i.p.) and did not further disrupt PPI. All three blockers protected GluN2A-N615S mice against AGS at 5 mg/kg (i.p.); only K2060 remained protective at 1 mg/kg (i.p.). Conclusions and Implications: Impaired Mg2+; block removes a physiological constraint on the action of NMDAR blockers. K2060 exhibited the most favourable pharmacological profile, supporting its further evaluation for studies with NMDAR hyperfunction models. Additional pharmacokinetic, safety, and disease-model studies are warranted.

title: The role of world knowledge in sentence comprehension under working-memory constraints: An fMRI study
abstract: Introduction: Comprehension of thematic roles, i.e., "who did what to whom," relies on limited cognitive resources, and constraints on these resources can alter the use of plausibility information derived from world knowledge. Although sentence-processing studies have described how plausibility information constrains interpretation, it remains unclear how this process is supported by the architecture of working memory. This study examines whether the phonological loop, one of the components of working memory, contributes to thematic-role processing based on world knowledge. Methods: Using articulatory suppression and functional magnetic resonance imaging, we examined whether constraining the function of the phonological loop modulates behavioral and neural responses to sentences in which syntactically assigned thematic roles are plausible or implausible given world knowledge. To constrain the phonological loop, we manipulated the task: a single task and a dual task involving concurrent articulation. Results: We found no significant interaction between task and plausibility, although equivalence analyses did not provide evidence for the absence of a plausibility effect during articulation. In contrast, a robust main effect of thematic-role plausibility was observed: implausible sentences elicited greater activation than plausible sentences in the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG) and medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) at the whole-brain level, and in both the pars triangularis and pars orbitalis of the LIFG in the ROI analyses. Discussion: These findings provide no conclusive evidence that constraining the phonological loop substantially modulates the use of world knowledge in comprehension of thematic roles, while also leaving open the possibility of a smaller task-dependent effect. At the same time, the robust neural responses to implausibility indicate that the LIFG and mSFG consistently contribute to the processing of plausibility information derived from world knowledge.

title: Attentional modulation of persistent visual representations after stimulus offset is coordinated across primary visual and anterior cingulate cortices
abstract: Flexible behavior in complex environments requires animals to infer which sensory inputs are relevant for guiding action and which need to be ignored. Yet, how cognitive control circuits apply contextual knowledge during decision-making is poorly understood. To address this question, we trained head-fixed mice on a cross-modal, context-dependent two-alternative forced-choice (2-AFC) decision-making task. In this task, animals simultaneously received visual and auditory inputs, and the behaviorally relevant modality switched covertly between blocks of trials, requiring animals to infer rule changes from reward feedback alone. Mice successfully adapted their behavior after rule switches and recovered to expert performance. Using simultaneous Neuropixels recordings in the primary visual cortex (V1) and the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) during task performance, we found that neuronal responses in both regions showed mixed selectivity, multiplexing sensory, choice, and outcome signals. However, V1 neural responses more strongly encoded visual stimulus orientation, while ACC neural responses preferentially encoded outcome. Population decoding further revealed that V1 and ACC neurons maintained a persistent representation of task context throughout the trial, occupying a subspace approximately orthogonal to visual stimulus coding. This contextual representation strengthened progressively as mice adapted their behavior following each switch. Critically, context representations emerged in parallel in V1 and ACC, and decoding accuracies in these two regions were strongly correlated with each other and with behavioral performance across trial blocks. Orthogonal to this shared emergent and sustained context signal, visual stimulus decoding was enhanced when vision was task-relevant. This attentional enhancement in V1 occurred not only during the stimulus presentation period but also after stimulus offset. Similarly, in ACC, a persistent increase of visual stimulus identity encoding in visually relevant session blocks was present after stimulus offset. Taken together, these findings reveal a distributed, inter-areal representation of task context spanning sensory and frontal cortices, suggesting that V1 and ACC contribute to maintaining task-relevant sensory information beyond the immediate sensory response period to provide a circuit-level mechanism for cross-modal attentional control.

title: Crowding distorts features, not objects: structured target confusions in a 4AFC conjunction task
abstract: Visual crowding is the disruption of peripheral object identification by nearby flanking clutter. It remains unclear whether crowding disrupts the bound representation of an object or degrades the object's component features separately. We addressed this with a 4AFC conjunction-report task in which observers reported both the orientation and the brightness of every target. Target Gabors at 6 degrees eccentricity were presented alone or flanked at 1, 3, or 5 degrees separation by Gabors varying independently in colour and/or orientation similarity to the target. We analysed the data three ways: joint accuracy, accuracy on each feature alone, and the statistical coupling between the two report channels. Orientation reports were principally impaired by orientation-similar flankers within the smallest target-flanker separations, whereas luminance reports were impaired by target-colour-similar flankers across a broader spatial range. Observed joint accuracy was closely predicted by the product of the two marginal accuracies in every condition. A complementary chi-square analysis of the full 4x4 stimulus-response matrices agreed with this conclusion at the most-crowded conditions, while revealing structured response biases that the ratio test could not detect. These biases were present at baseline and were not amplified by crowding. The conjunction errors observed under crowding therefore arose from two largely independent feature-specific failures, rather than from disruption of a representation in which the two features are bound. These results indicate that object-level crowding errors in this paradigm are the downstream signature of two independent feature-level processes rather than the breakdown of an object-level mechanism.

title: The effect of preproenkephalin gene deletion on heart function in mice
abstract: Enkephalins, the endogenous ligands of the - and {delta}-opioid receptors, are abundantly expressed in the nervous system and peripheral organs, including the heart. Accumulating evidence suggests that they participate in cardiac development and act as autocrine and paracrine modulators of heart activity. Here, we investigate the role of enkephalins in cardiac physiology using a newly generated mouse strain with a complete ablation of the preproenkephalin (Penk) gene. We find that, although adult mutant mice weighed less, the mutation caused no apparent changes in behavioral phenotype, no increase in anxiety-like behaviors, and only a mild reduction in locomotor activity. There was no effect of Penk deletion on heart weight or size. A comprehensive analysis of left ventricular function using MRI revealed normal basal cardiac performance, except for a significant reduction in the peak fill and ejection rates. There were no significant effects of Penk deletion on left ventricular function after {beta}1-adrenergic stimulation with dobutamine. At the same time, we observed the expected significant differences in heart size and function between male and female mice. In conclusion, our data show that enkephalins are not essential for normal heart development and have a moderate impact on adult heart function under basal conditions.

title: Separation, isolation, and membrane lipid profiling of selectively vulnerable and resilient neurons
abstract: Certain neurons are more susceptible to pathogenic stressors and degenerate, while others remain resilient in neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms underlying this cell-to-cell heterogeneity in neuronal vulnerability remain unclear, primarily due to challenges in isolating vulnerable and resilient neurons to characterize their properties. In this study, we report the development of a novel cell-labeling method utilizing two cell-impermeable dyes to identify vulnerable and resilient neurons in culture, which are subsequently separated and isolated via fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS). As a proof-of-concept of a mechanistic study, we conducted lipidomic analysis to determine whether the lipid composition of membranes differs between vulnerable and resilient neurons to oxidative stress. This simple but unique method sets the groundwork for investigating the molecular underpinnings of selective neuronal vulnerability, which could inform new diagnostic strategies and therapeutic targets for neurodegenerative diseases.

title: ZFP36 is a post-transcriptional regulator of the P2X4 receptor in myeloid cells
abstract: P2X4 is an ATP-gated purinergic receptor upregulated in spinal microglia after peripheral nerve injury, where it plays a key role in neuropathic pain. Yet, the molecular mechanisms controlling P2X4 expression remain incompletely understood. To address this question, we examined P2X4 mRNA expression and translation in spinal microglia following nerve injury. While total P2X4 mRNA levels remained unchanged, ribosome-associated P2X4 mRNA increased, revealing a previously unrecognized level of translational regulation. We therefore investigated whether the RNA-binding protein ZFP36 (tristetraprolin), a well-established regulator of inflammatory mRNAs, controls P2X4 expression. Our results demonstrate that the P2X4 3'UTR strongly repressed reporter and protein expression and that ZFP36 emerged as a negative regulator of P2X4 mRNA. This regulation involved phosphorylation-dependent signaling through p38 MAPK and 14-3-3. Moreover, ZFP36 knockdown increased P2X4 protein expression, while manipulation of ZFP36 phosphorylation altered P2X4-dependent ATP-evoked calcium responses. Together, these findings identify ZFP36 as a previously unrecognized post-transcriptional regulator of P2X4, extending its role beyond inflammatory mediators to a functional purinergic receptor. They reveal post-transcriptional control of receptor availability as a novel regulatory layer linking myeloid cell state to purinergic responsiveness and provide a new framework for understanding microglial P2X4 regulation in neuropathic pain.

title: Dual Roles of Interferon-γ Receptor in Somatostatin Interneurons at Baseline and During Inflammation
abstract: Background: Neuropsychiatric disorders such as major depressive disorder show converging evidence of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) dysfunction, including consistent reductions in somatostatin (SST) interneuron markers. SST interneurons are selectively vulnerable to inflammation, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Interferon-gamma (IFN-{gamma}), a pro-inflammatory cytokine implicated in mood and anxiety disorders, signals through the IFN-{gamma} receptor (IFNGR), which is expressed in neurons. We tested whether IFNGR signaling in SST interneurons regulates anxiety-like and cognitive behavior and prevents inflammation-induced molecular deficits. Methods: We generated mice with conditional deletion of IFNGR from SST cells and assessed anxiety-like behavior using elevated plus maze and working memory using Y-maze at baseline and after lipopolysaccharide (LPS) induced inflammation. Expression of SST-related, neurotrophic, synaptic, and glial markers was quantified. Results: At baseline and after LPS-induced inflammation, IFNGR deletion in SST cells increased anxiety-like behavior without affecting working memory. In control mice, LPS reduced Sst (p=0.0006), neuropeptide Y (Npy) (p=0.0022), brain-derived neurotrophic factor (Bdnf) (p<0.0001), and synapsin 1 (Syn1) (p=0.0150); these reductions were not significant in mice lacking IFNGR in SST cells. Knockouts also showed lower baseline Bdnf, Syn1, Gephyrin (Gphn), and allograft inflammatory factor 1 (Aif1, encoding Iba1) than controls. Conclusions: IFNGR signaling in SST cells plays a dual role: supporting normal behavior and molecular homeostasis while mediating LPS-induced molecular deficits. These findings link immune signaling to the GABAergic dysfunction implicated in major depressive disorder and suggest IFNGR signaling in SST cells may regulate cortical microcircuit integrity at baseline and during inflammatory challenge.
